clinicalPearls: Umbrella term for germline variants in the succinate dehydrogenase genes (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD) and the assembly factor SDHAF2 predisposing to paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas, historically designated PGL1–5.
SDHD (PGL1) and SDHAF2 (PGL2) show maternal imprinting, so tumours arise almost exclusively when the mutant allele is inherited from the father.
Head and neck paragangliomas (carotid body, jugulotympanic, vagal) are typically parasympathetic and non-secretory, presenting as a painless neck mass or with cranial nerve palsies.
Sympathetic thoraco-abdominal paragangliomas and adrenal phaeochromocytomas secrete catecholamines, causing paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension.
Biochemical screening relies on plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines; a noradrenergic and dopaminergic profile with raised normetanephrine and methoxytyramine is characteristic.
Loss of SDHB immunohistochemical staining in tumour tissue flags an underlying SDHx defect regardless of which subunit gene is mutated.
SDHB variants carry the highest risk of metastatic disease, whereas SDHD more often produces multifocal head and neck tumours.
Associated neoplasms include SDH-deficient gastrointestinal stromal tumour, renal cell carcinoma and pituitary adenoma (the '3PAs' association).
reference.pathophysiology: The succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) complex, mitochondrial complex II, links the tricarboxylic acid cycle to the electron transport chain by oxidising succinate to fumarate. A germline loss-of-function variant in a subunit or the assembly factor SDHAF2, followed by somatic loss of the wild-type allele, abolishes enzyme activity and destabilises the whole complex, so SDHB protein is lost on immunohistochemistry irrespective of the gene involved. Accumulated succinate behaves as an oncometabolite, inhibiting alpha-ketoglutarate–dependent prolyl hydroxylases and other dioxygenases; this stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, driving a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic transcriptional programme, and causes widespread DNA and histone hypermethylation. Neural crest–derived chromaffin and paraganglionic cells are especially vulnerable, giving catecholamine-secreting or non-secretory tumours according to their sympathetic or parasympathetic origin. Maternal imprinting of the SDHD and SDHAF2 loci explains the parent-of-origin transmission pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary PPGL genes (MAX, TMEM127, FH, EPAS1/HIF2A)
Non-syndromic carotid body or glomus tumour
additionalInvestigations: Plasma free or fractionated urinary metanephrines including methoxytyramine
Germline testing with a hereditary PPGL gene panel and cascade testing of relatives
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of neck, thorax, abdomen and pelvis for localisation
Functional imaging with Ga-DOTATATE PET (particularly sensitive in SDHx disease) or MIBG scintigraphy
SDHB immunohistochemistry on resected tumour tissue
Audiometry and cranial nerve assessment for head and neck paragangliomas
A structured lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance protocol for carriers
redFlags: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with labile or severe hypertension suggesting a catecholamine crisis
Rapidly enlarging neck mass with new cranial nerve palsy or dysphagia
Features of metastatic disease such as bone pain or weight loss, especially in SDHB carriers
Unopposed catecholamine surge during anaesthesia or tumour manipulation without adequate blockade
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on genotype, tumour location and secretory status; completely resected non-metastatic tumours carry a good outlook, whereas SDHB-associated metastatic disease substantially reduces survival. Lifelong surveillance is required because of multifocal and metachronous tumour risk.
pitfalls: Attributing a solitary head and neck paraganglioma to sporadic disease and omitting germline testing.
Overlooking dopamine or methoxytyramine-secreting tumours that lack classic adrenergic symptoms and may appear biochemically silent on standard testing.
Proceeding to surgery or biopsy of a secretory tumour without adequate preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade.
Forgetting the parent-of-origin effect when counselling SDHD or SDHAF2 families, in whom maternal transmission is usually silent.
Relying on MIBG imaging alone, which is less sensitive than somatostatin-receptor PET in SDHx-related disease.
management: Prepare secretory tumours for resection with alpha-adrenergic blockade followed by beta-blockade and volume repletion to avert a perioperative hypertensive crisis
Offer surgical excision as definitive treatment, but for head-and-neck parasympathetic paragangliomas weigh surgery against radiotherapy or surveillance because of the risk of cranial nerve morbidity
Screen biochemically with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines including methoxytyramine
Treat metastatic and SDHB-related disease with radionuclide therapy such as Ga-DOTATATE-based peptide receptor radionuclide therapy or MIBG, chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Provide audiological and cranial nerve monitoring for head-and-neck tumours and maintain lifelong imaging and biochemical surveillance for multifocal and metachronous disease
Offer genetic counselling recognising the maternal imprinting of SDHD and SDHAF2, with cascade testing of relatives
